audience: HTTP/API engineers learning to reason about a Load Balancer component in an interview-sized architecture.
prerequisites: An HTTP client sends a request to a server and receives a response; a network connection can carry requests.
An API server can read or write a database. A transaction commits related writes together or aborts them; a committed write can remain stored even if the caller does not receive a response.

objectives.description: Define a backend as an application server selected to handle traffic. Trace a request and response through a reverse-proxy load balancer, explain the stable entry point and traffic distribution, and identify when a single adequate backend makes balancing unnecessary.

Define L4 as transport-level connection routing and L7 as application-level HTTP routing. Explain connection selection versus HTTP-aware selection, the need for access to HTTP contents, and why adding HTTP requests on one existing connection need not spread L4 traffic.

Explain round robin (take turns), least connections (choose fewer active connections), and weights (bias the share). Choose using workload assumptions and explain why request count or connection count is only a proxy for actual work.

Define a health check as a sampled signal and readiness as ability to accept useful new work. Explain removing an unhealthy backend from new selections, detection delay, imperfect endpoint checks, and why removal cannot rescue an already failed request.

Define session state as information retained between a user's requests and affinity or stickiness as preferring the same backend. Explain local-state failure across replicas, the tradeoffs of affinity versus shared state, and why affinity does not replicate state or guarantee failover.

Define draining as stopping new assigned work while allowing already accepted work to finish within a deadline. Explain deployment order, in-flight work (requests already underway), forced termination at a deadline, and why connection versus HTTP-request routing changes what must be drained.

Explain why a lost response creates an unknown operation outcome. Define an idempotency key as a stable identifier for one logical operation and deduplication as recognizing repeats; explain bounded retry cost and durable, atomic coordination between a write and its duplicate record across backends.

Distinguish traffic distribution from creating capacity. Explain backend headroom (spare capacity), downstream bottlenecks, the balancer as a possible single failure point, and the need for a reachable alternate entry path and sufficient surviving capacity during failure.

questions.question: A ticketing API has a reverse-proxy balancer and two application servers. Clients reuse one connection for many HTTP requests; the team wants /search and /purchase routed to different server pools. Trace the request and response path through this proxy. Choose L4 or L7 for path-based routing, state what HTTP visibility it needs, and explain why one reused L4 connection does not imply distribution of its individual requests. Also state when a single adequate server might make a balancer unnecessary.
criteria: Traces client to balancer to selected backend and response through the reverse proxy to the client.
Chooses L7 for HTTP-path routing and requires visibility into the HTTP request, including decryption where needed.
Explains that L4 typically selects a backend for a connection rather than independently selecting for each HTTP request carried on it.
Explains that distribution or availability needs can justify the extra component, while one adequate server without those needs may not need it.
criticalMisconceptions: L4 inherently routes on HTTP paths.
Every HTTP request on a reused L4 connection must select a fresh backend.

questions.question: A ticketing service mixes cheap seat lookups with long requests; one backend is twice as capable as another. Compare round robin, least connections, and weighted selection for these facts, naming what each measures or controls and one limitation of each. The shared database is then saturated: explain why another backend alone may not raise throughput. Finally, explain what must be true of the balancer entry path and surviving backend capacity for service to remain available after one machine fails.
criteria: Round robin takes turns but does not account for unequal work or backend capacity; least connections uses active connection count but connections may carry unequal work; weights bias traffic shares toward capacity but are not a live guarantee of capacity or performance.
Makes a conditional choice consistent with workload facts rather than claiming one algorithm always wins.
Explains that more application servers do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck or create capacity merely by balancing traffic.

Requires an available alternate balancer entry path if the balancer fails and sufficient surviving backend headroom if a backend fails; redundancy alone does not guarantee availability under overload.
criticalMisconceptions: Balanced request counts guarantee balanced work.
Adding a balancer creates processing capacity.
Two backends eliminate the balancer as a possible single failure point.

questions.question: A ticketing backend's health endpoint returns 200 while its purchase handler cannot access a required database. Checks run periodically. Explain why a check that reflects readiness matters, why even an improved check cannot detect every failure immediately, what removing the backend changes for new traffic, and what it cannot repair for requests already underway.
criteria: Distinguishes a responding endpoint from readiness to perform useful requested work; a relevant check must reflect required capabilities rather than just process existence.
Explains sampling delay and imperfect coverage or failures occurring after a successful check.
Removal prevents new selections after detection rather than guaranteeing that no request reaches a failing backend.
Already underway requests can still fail; removal does not complete, undo, or safely replay them.
criticalMisconceptions: A passing health check proves all requests will succeed.
Health checks instantly prevent failed requests.

questions.question: A ticket customer's cart lives only in server A's memory. A later request goes to B, or A fails. Explain both outcomes. Compare sticky routing with shared session storage, including one cost of each, and explain whether stickiness copies the cart or guarantees it survives A's failure.
criteria: B lacks A's memory-only cart; failure of A can lose the only available copy.
Affinity can keep normal requests on A but can skew distribution and restrict placement; it neither copies state nor guarantees recovery on failure.
Shared session storage lets either backend access the cart but adds a shared dependency and access or coordination cost; its own availability still matters.
criticalMisconceptions: Sticky sessions replicate state.
Affinity guarantees session survival when the preferred server fails.

questions.question: During a ticketing deployment, server A has an accepted 20-second request and a reused client connection. Describe the order for draining A and shutting it down, how new assignments differ from accepted work, and what happens when the drain deadline expires. Explain why merely stopping new L4 connections may still allow more HTTP requests on an existing connection and why draining must address the actual routing unit.
criteria: Stops new assignments before termination and allows accepted work to finish within a defined deadline.
Distinguishes new traffic from in-flight work; terminating at the deadline can interrupt remaining work and does not guarantee every request completes.
Existing L4 connections can carry further HTTP requests, so draining must handle existing connection lifetimes or request acceptance; L7 request-aware draining must likewise manage accepted requests.
criticalMisconceptions: Removing a backend from new selection immediately makes it safe to kill.
Stopping new connections necessarily stops all new HTTP requests.

questions.question: A purchase transaction commits on A, but its response is lost. A retry may be sent to B. Explain why the timeout leaves the client uncertain and why blind retry can create a duplicate purchase. Describe how the same idempotency key, a durable duplicate record shared across backends, and atomic coordination with the purchase write can make a repeat return the recorded result without repeating the effect. Explain why a fresh key per retry or A-only memory is insufficient, and why retries should have limits and delay during overload.
criteria: A timeout does not prove the purchase failed; an unprotected repeat can commit another purchase.
Reuses one key for one logical operation and lets all relevant backends recognize its durable recorded outcome.

Coordinates the duplicate record and purchase effect atomically so a crash or concurrent repeat cannot leave a committed effect unrecognized; a new key or A-only memory cannot reliably recognize the repeat on B.
Limits retry attempts and delays retries because extra attempts consume capacity and can worsen overload; retries alone do not guarantee success or safety.
criticalMisconceptions: A missing response proves that no write committed.
A load balancer makes any write safe to retry.
A key by itself guarantees duplicate prevention without coordinated durable state.

cards.objective: Trace a reverse-proxy request and response through a stable entry point and selected backend; explain distribution and when it is unnecessary.

questions.question: A catalog API places a reverse-proxy balancer before two servers. Trace a request and its response, explain what the balancer selects and why the entry point is useful, and give a condition under which one server could be enough without balancing.
criteria: Traces client, balancer, selected backend, and response via the proxy.
Explains distribution behind one entry point and that one adequate server can suffice without a need for distribution or redundant serving.
criticalMisconceptions: The balancer must execute the application's database operation itself.

cards.objective: Compare connection-level L4 selection with HTTP-aware L7 selection, including HTTP visibility and reused connections.

questions.question: A catalog client sends many requests on one connection. Choose L4 or L7 to route /images separately from /orders, state the visibility required, and explain whether L4 must distribute those individual requests across servers.
criteria: Chooses L7 and requires access to HTTP paths, including decryption where necessary.
Explains that L4 selection is for the connection, so its requests need not be separately balanced.
criticalMisconceptions: L4 connection balancing automatically inspects HTTP paths.

cards.objective: Choose among round robin, least connections and weights using workload assumptions; explain each signal's limits.

questions.question: Catalog requests have uneven durations and servers have unequal capacity. Compare how round robin, least connections, and weights select traffic; identify one limitation of each and give a conditional choice for this workload.
criteria: Explains turns, active connection counts, and biased traffic shares respectively.
Explains unequal work defeats equal turns, connection counts need not reflect work, and configured weights cannot guarantee live performance.
Gives a conditional choice tied to request duration or server capacity, without claiming a universally best algorithm.
criticalMisconceptions: Equal counts imply equal processing load.

cards.objective: Use readiness checks to limit new traffic to unhealthy backends while explaining detection delay, imperfect coverage and in-flight failures.

questions.question: A catalog server answers a periodic /health request but cannot serve catalog data. Explain readiness versus a responding endpoint, why an improved check still has delay and blind spots, what removing the server changes for new assignments, and what it cannot fix for requests already underway.
criteria: Readiness concerns useful work, not merely a responding process.
Periodic samples and limited coverage cannot prove immediate or universal health.
Removal limits new selection after detection but cannot rescue work already underway.
criticalMisconceptions: Passing health checks guarantees every request succeeds.

cards.objective: Explain local session state across replicas and compare affinity with shared state, including costs and failover limits.

questions.question: A catalog shopping session exists only in A's memory. Explain what happens if the next request goes to B or A fails; compare affinity and shared storage with one cost each, and state whether affinity copies or preserves that state after A fails.
criteria: B cannot access A-only memory and losing A can lose its session.
Affinity prefers A but can skew load; shared storage enables access from either backend but adds a dependency and access or coordination cost.
Affinity neither replicates state nor guarantees recovery after A fails.
criticalMisconceptions: Stickiness is state replication.

cards.objective: Plan graceful removal using new-assignment cutoff, accepted-work completion and a deadline while distinguishing connection and HTTP-request draining.

questions.question: A catalog server must restart while a request is underway on a reused connection. State the drain and shutdown order, what a deadline means for unfinished work, and why stopping new L4 connections alone may still permit additional HTTP requests on existing connections.
criteria: Stops new assignments, allows already accepted work to finish, then shuts down when complete or the deadline expires.
Deadline termination may interrupt unfinished requests.
Existing connections may carry further requests, so draining must address connection lifetime or request acceptance rather than assume no new connections means no new requests.
criticalMisconceptions: Draining guarantees all in-flight work finishes.

cards.objective: Reason about an unknown write outcome and safe repeated operations using one stable key, shared durable deduplication coordinated atomically with the effect, and bounded delayed retries.

questions.question: A catalog order commits but its response is lost; the retry reaches another server. Explain the unknown outcome and duplicate risk, describe the stable key and shared durable duplicate record atomically coordinated with the order write, explain why new retry keys or memory on only the first server fail, and explain why retries need limits and delay.
criteria: A lost response does not prove failure and unprotected retry can duplicate the order.
Reuses one operation key and makes a durable recorded result accessible across backends with atomic coordination of record and effect.
A new key does not identify the repeat and memory on only one server does not protect a retry on another.
Limits and delay reduce extra load during failures or overload without promising eventual success.
criticalMisconceptions: All timed-out writes are safe to retry.
An idempotency key alone prevents duplicate effects.

cards.objective: Explain the limits of balancing, surviving headroom, shared downstream bottlenecks and availability of the balancer entry path itself.

questions.question: A catalog API has two backends, one balancer, and a saturated shared database. Explain why adding balancing or another backend need not increase throughput. Explain what must be true of the entry path if the balancer fails and of surviving backend capacity if a backend fails, and why redundancy alone does not guarantee available service.
criteria: Balancing distributes existing work capacity and extra backends do not remove the saturated shared database bottleneck.
Balancer failure requires a reachable alternate entry path; backend failure requires enough surviving headroom for the remaining load.
Redundant components can still overload or depend on failed shared components, so redundancy alone does not guarantee availability.
criticalMisconceptions: A balancer creates application or database capacity.
Two backends make a single balancer failure harmless.
